hypothesis: Decomposing a VLA policy into a separate arm expert and a higher-rate hand expert improves dexterous grasp success over a monolithic decoder.
experiment: Train both the decomposed and monolithic policies on the same 500-demo dataset with identical backbone, optimizer, and schedule. Evaluate on 4 held-out objects across 50 real-robot trials each; report grasp success with 95% CIs and an ablation that removes the rate separation.

hypothesis: A heterogeneous body/hand action expert is better than a single decoder.
experiment: We train our method and show it works well on a few grasping tasks in simulation. Results look promising.

hypothesis: Binding tactile input at finger-level granularity rather than flat concatenation improves contact-rich insertion.
experiment: Compare finger-level binding vs. flat-concat tactile encoding with matched parameter count. Run 60 real-robot peg-insertion trials per condition over 3 seeds; report success rate, insertion time, and an ablation over the number of tactile channels.
We add a tactile sensor to the gripper and observe qualitatively that grasps seem more stable in a demo video. No quantitative comparison is reported.

hypothesis: A scoped low-level RL hand-stabilization module reduces contact-force spikes without degrading the high-level policy.
experiment: Measure peak contact force and task success with and without the System0 module across 80 trials on 2 robots. Include a baseline of pure position control and an ablation that varies the RL reward weighting; report force distributions, not just means.

hypothesis: Reinforcement learning makes hands more robust.
experiment: Train an RL policy in simulation with a custom reward. Report final reward curve. No baseline, no real-robot evaluation, no ablation on the reward terms.

hypothesis: Preserving VLM pretraining via a forward-KL carve-out loss during fine-tuning retains language grounding while learning manipulation.
experiment: Fine-tune with and without the carve-out loss; evaluate manipulation success AND a held-out VQA probe set to measure forgetting. Three seeds, report both axes with significance tests and an ablation over the KL weight.

hypothesis: Our fine-tuning recipe avoids catastrophic forgetting.
experiment: We fine-tune the model and it still answers one example question correctly. We conclude forgetting is solved.

hypothesis: A falsifiable task definition with a pre-registered success threshold yields more reproducible sim-to-real transfer numbers.
experiment: Define the task and threshold before runs; execute 100 real-robot trials across 2 labs with the same protocol; report inter-lab variance and compare against an unregistered baseline protocol.

hypothesis: Our method achieves state-of-the-art sim-to-real transfer.
experiment: We report a single best-of-many success number on one object in one lab, tuned after seeing the test set. No variance, no baseline, no held-out protocol.

hypothesis: Real-time action chunking with delayed-horizon correction reduces jerk in high-frequency hand control.
experiment: Benchmark jerk and tracking error vs. a no-chunking baseline and a fixed-chunk baseline on 3 trajectories, 5 seeds, with an ablation sweeping the correction horizon; report distributions and statistical tests.

hypothesis: Bigger models always help dexterous manipulation.
experiment: We train one large model and one small model on different datasets with different schedules and report that the large one had a higher number on a different benchmark. The comparison is not controlled.
